title: Almost no flight data where the Moon base will live
text: Of 1,647 flight-test records with an ambient O₂ and pressure (718 measured, the rest run in ISS cabin air), 37 sit inside the lunar-base envelope (≥28% O₂, ≤0.75 atm), all from CFI-G normal, FLEX. No solid-material test exceeds 22.7% O₂ and none was flown at reduced pressure. Spacesuit conditions (100% O₂, 4.3 psi): 0 tests.
implication: The highest-value next flight experiment is solid-material flammability at ≥30% O₂ and ≤10.2 psi.

title: Lunar-base air makes self-extinction ~11× less likely than cabin air
text: The validated FLEX model gives a methanol droplet flame a 72% chance of self-extinguishing in cabin air (21%, 1 atm) and 6% at 30% O₂ and 10.2 psi (90% interval 2%–14%). Out-of-sample AUC 0.88 with whole test days held out.
implication: Material screening done for 21% / 1 atm cannot be reused for the Moon base without re-testing.

title: Solid-material data is dominated by one plastic
text: 177 of 238 solid-material tests (candles excluded) are PMMA; Nomex, silicone and Ultem together have 16.
implication: Cabin fabrics and polymers other than PMMA need flight data before any envelope can be trusted.

title: Above 30% O₂, flames stop putting themselves out
text: In FLEX, 24 droplet fires burned at 30–34% O₂ (17 of them at 0.70 atm, next to the lunar-base atmosphere). Only 2 self-extinguished — 0 of the 17 at 0.70 atm — against 73 of 79 below 18% O₂.
implication: A fire on a lunar base must be detected and actively suppressed; waiting for it to die out is not an option.

title: Helium and larger droplets push flames toward extinction
text: Holding everything else fixed, adding helium raises the odds of self-extinction (standardized effect +0.47, 90% CI +0.23 to +0.93); so does a larger initial droplet (+0.81), consistent with radiative-loss extinction of large microgravity flames.
implication: Diluent choice matters: helium-rich atmospheres change fire behavior, not only O₂ level.

title: CO₂ dilution suppresses droplet fires at reduced pressure
text: At 0.7 atm, droplet flames self-extinguished in 50% of tests without CO₂ (n=46) and in 100% with >30% CO₂ (n=22). Once O₂ is accounted for, the model attributes a smaller, uncertain effect to CO₂ — CO₂ tests were often run at different O₂ levels.
implication: CO₂ works, but its effect is confounded with O₂ in FLEX: a controlled CO₂ series at lunar-base O₂ is needed.

title: One limiting flame temperature? Only for normal gas flames
text: For ACME CFI-G normal flames, self-extinction becomes more likely as adiabatic flame temperature drops (AUC 0.70). The 50% point, ≈ 2,858 K (90% CI 2,749–3,171 K), lies just above the hottest normal flame tested (2,730 K), so it is an extrapolation. For inverse flames the same single-variable rule has no predictive power (AUC 0.46).
implication: Flame temperature alone is not a universal extinction criterion; geometry and flow matter.

title: Smoke differs by material, and ages before it reaches a detector
text: SAME and SAME-R measured smoke from Kapton, Teflon, silicone, Pyrell and lamp wick in orbit, including how particle size grows with aging time (109 SAME-R tests, 8 SAME).
implication: Detector thresholds should be set per material and per transport time, not from 1-g smoke.

title: Cool flames: invisible fire, confirmed in orbit
text: 7 cool flames were confirmed in ACME CFI-G, all with 30% butane near 40% O₂ and 2.0 atm. They burn at low temperature with almost no visible light.
implication: Optical flame detectors can miss cool flames; chemical (CO, aldehyde) sensing is a candidate complement.

title: At 20 cm/s, the 1-g test was the more severe one
text: Saffire-II burned the same samples in orbit and on the ground: in 8 of 8 single-material samples, 1 g burned as much or more than microgravity (silicone barely spread in orbit but burned fully on the ground). BASS's concern — that 1-g screening may not be conservative — applies to low-flow conditions Saffire-II did not test.
implication: μg and 1-g results bound partial gravity only for the flow regime that was tested; low-flow is the open question.

title: Concurrent airflow made a large fire burn 6× longer
text: In Saffire-I the same 94 × 40 cm SIBAL fabric burned for 420 s with concurrent flow and 70 s with opposed flow, both at 20 cm/s and ~21.5% O₂.
implication: Cabin ventilation direction defines the worst case; fan layout is a fire-safety design variable.
